source_text: Τοὐναντίον μὲν οὖν ἐῤῥώσθησαν τοῖς κινδύνοις, καὶ φιλοτιμότεροι γεγόνασιν εἰς εὐσέβειαν. Τοιοῦτο γὰρ τὸ παθεῖν ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ, τῷ φίλτρῳ προστίθησι, καὶ οἷον ἀῤῥαβὼν γίνεται τῶν ἑξῆς ἄθλων τοῖς μεγαλόφροσι. Τοιαῦτά σου, Αἴγυπτε, τὰ νῦν διηγήματά τε καὶ θαύματα. Εʹ. Σὺ δέ μοι τοὺς τράγους ἐπῄνεις τοὺς Μενδησίους, καὶ τὸν Μεμφίτην Ἄπιν, μόσχον σιτευτόν τινα καὶ πολύσαρκον, καὶ τὰς Ἴσιδος τελετὰς, καὶ τοὺς Ὀσίριδος σπαραγμοὺς, καὶ τὸν σεμνόν σου Σάραπιν, ξύλον προσκυνούμενον μετὰ μύθου, καὶ χρόνου, καὶ τῆς τῶν προσκυνούντων ἀνοίας, ὡς ὕλην ἄγνωστόν τινα καὶ οὐράνιον, πλὴν ὕλην, κἂν βοηθῆται τῷ ψεύ δει· καὶ τὰ ἔτι τούτων αἰσχρότερα, κνωδάλων τινῶν καὶ ἑρπετῶν πολυειδῆ πλάσματα, ὧν πάντων ὑπερ ῆρε Χριστὸς, καὶ οἱ Χριστοῦ κήρυκες· ἄλλοι τε ἄλ λως κατὰ τοὺς ἑαυτῶν ἕκαστοι χρόνους ἐκλάμψαντες· καὶ δὴ καὶ οἱ νῦν μνημονευθέντες Πατέρες· ἀφ' ὧν σὺ γινώσκῃ μᾶλλον, ὦ θαυμασία, σήμερον, ἢ πάντων ὁμοῦ πάντες, καὶ παλαιῶν καὶ νέων διηγημάτων. ςʹ. Διὰ ταῦτά σε περιπτύσσομαι καὶ ἀσπάζομαι, λαῶν ἄριστε, καὶ φιλοχριστότατε, καὶ θερμότατε τὴν εὐσέβειαν, καὶ τῶν ἀγόντων ἄξιε· οὐ γὰρ ἔχω τι τού του μεῖζον εἰπεῖν, οὐδὲ ᾧ μᾶλλον ἂν ὑμᾶς ξενίσαιμι· καὶ δεξιοῦμαι, ὀλίγα μὲν γλώσσῃ, τὰ πολλὰ δὲ δια νοίας κινήμασι. Λαὸς ἐμός· ἐμὸν γὰρ ὀνομάζω, τὸν ὁμόφρονα καὶ ὁμόδοξον, καὶ παρὰ τῶν αὐτῶν Πατέρων, καὶ τῆς αὐτῆς Τριάδος προσκυνητήν. Λαὸς ἐμός· ἐμὸς γὰρ, κἂν μὴ δοκῇ τοῖς βασκαίνουσι· καὶ, ἵνα πληγῶσι μᾶλλον οἱ τοῦτο πάσχοντες, ἰδοὺ δίδωμι δεξιὰς κοινωνίας ἐπὶ τοσούτων μαρτύρων, ὁρατῶν τε καὶ ἀοράτων· καὶ ἀπωθοῦμαι παλαιὰν διαβολὴν νέᾳ χρηστότητι. Λαὸς ἐμός· ἐμὸς γὰρ, εἰ καὶ τὸν μέγιστον ὁ μικρότατος σφετερίζομαι. Τοιαύτη γὰρ ἡ τοῦ Πνεύματος χάρις· ὁμοτίμους ποιεῖ τοὺς ὁμόφρονας. Λαὸς ἐμός· ἐμὸς γὰρ, εἰ καὶ πόῤῥωθεν· ὅτι θεϊκῶς συναπτόμεθα, καὶ τρόπον ἄλλον, ἢ ὃν αἱ παχύτητες. Τὰ μὲν γὰρ σώματα τόπῳ συνάπτεται, ψυ χαὶ δὲ Πνεύματι συναρμόζονται. Λαὸς ἐμὸς, ὁ πρότερον μὲν φιλοσοφῶν τὸ πάσχειν ὑπὲρ Χριστοῦ, νῦν δὲ τὸ μὴ ποιεῖν, ἐὰν ἐμοὶ πείθησθε, ἀλλ' αὔταρ κες κέρδος τίθεσθαι τὴν τοῦ ποιεῖν ἐξουσίαν, καὶ ἡγεῖσθαι Χριστῷ λατρείαν εἰσφέρειν, ὥσπερ τότε τὴν καρτερίαν, οὕτως ἐν τῷ παρόντι τὴν ἐπιείκειαν. Λαὸς, ἐφ' ὃν παρατέτακται ὁ Κύριος τοῦ εὖ ποιῆσαι, ὥσπερ τοῦ κακοποιῆσαι τοὺς ἐναντίους. Λαὸς, ὃν ἐξελέξατο ἑαυτῷ Κύριος ἐκ πάντων ὧν προσεκαλέσατο. Λαὸς, ὁ ἐπὶ τῶν χειρῶν Κυρίου ἐζωγραφημένος, ᾧ, Σὺ γὰρ εἶ θέλημα ἐμὸν, λέγει Κύριος· καὶ, Αἱ πύλαι σου γλύμμα· καὶ ὅσα τοῖς σωζομένοις ὕστερον. Λαὸς, καὶ μή με θαυμάσητε τῆς ἀπληστίας, εἰ πολλάκις ὑμᾶς ἀναστρέφω· κατατρυφῶ γὰρ ὑμῶν τῇ συνεχείᾳ τῆς κλήσεως, ὥσπερ οἱ θεαμάτων τινῶν, ἢ ἀκουσμάτων ἀπλήστως ἐμφορούμενοι. Ζʹ. Ἀλλ', ὦ Θεοῦ λαὸς, καὶ ἡμέτερος, καλὴ μὲν ὑμῶν καὶ ἡ πρώην πανήγυρις, ἣν ἐπὶ τῆς θα λάσσης ἐστήσασθε, καὶ εἴπερ ἄλλη τις ὀφθαλμῶν χάρις, ἡνίκα εἶδον δενδρουμένην τὴν θάλασσαν, καὶ χειροποιήτῳ νέφει κεκαλυμμένην, καὶ κάλλος νηῶν, καὶ τάχος, ὥσπερ εἰς πομπὴν ἐσταλμένων, καὶ πνεῦμα μέτριον κατὰ πρύμναν ἱστάμενον, ὥσπερ δορυφοροῦν ἐξεπίτηδες, καὶ παραπέμπον τῇ πόλει πόλιν πελάγιον· καλλίων δὲ ἡ νῦν ὁρωμένη καὶ μεγαλοπρεπεστέρα.
thought_title: Egypt's old idols replaced by a faithful people
orientation: Gregory contrasts Egypt's former animal and idol cults with the present orthodox Egyptians whom he embraces as his own people.
pass_a_gloss: On the contrary, they were strengthened by the dangers, and have become more zealous toward reverence. For such a thing is suffering for Christ: it adds to love, and becomes like a pledge of the contests that follow for the great-minded. Such are your present narratives and wonders, O Egypt. But you praised to me the Mendesian goats, and the Memphite Apis, some fatted and fleshy calf, and the rites of Isis, and the dismemberments of Osiris, and your august Serapis, wood worshipped with myth and time and the folly of the worshippers, as some unknown and heavenly matter, but matter, even if aided by falsehood; and things still more shameful than these, variegated fabrications of certain beasts and creeping things, all of which Christ surpassed, and the heralds of Christ surpassed, both others having shone forth in different ways each in their own times, and indeed also the Fathers now mentioned; from whom you may know rather, O marvelous one, today, than all people together know from all narratives together, both old and new. For these reasons I embrace you and greet you, best of peoples, and most loving Christ, and most fervent in reverence, and worthy of those leading you; for I have nothing greater than this to say, nor with what I might rather entertain you as guests; and I receive you with right hands, few things with the tongue, but most things with movements of thought. My people; for I name as mine the one of like mind and like belief, and worshiper of the same Fathers and of the same Trinity. My people; for mine, even if it does not seem so to the enviers; and, so that those who suffer this may be struck still more, behold I give right hands of fellowship before so many witnesses, both visible and invisible; and I thrust away an old slander with a new kindness. My people; for mine, even if I, smallest, claim as my own the greatest. For such is the grace of the Spirit: it makes those of like mind equal in honor. My people; for mine, even if from far off; because we are joined together divinely, and in another way than thick bodies are. For bodies are joined by place, but souls are fitted together by the Spirit. My people, who formerly practiced suffering for Christ, but now, if you are persuaded by me, practice not doing evil, but rather count as gain the power to do good, and consider that you bring in service to Christ, just as then endurance, so in the present gentleness. A people, for whose benefit the Lord has been arrayed in battle order to do good, just as to do evil to the opponents. A people, whom the Lord chose for himself out of all whom he called. A people, portrayed on the hands of the Lord, to whom, 'For you are my delight,' says the Lord; and, 'Your gates are a carving'; and as many things as afterward belong to those being saved. A people, and do not marvel at me for greediness, if I turn you over often; for I delight in the continuity of your calling, just as those who insatiably gorge themselves on certain sights or hearings. But, O people of God, and ours, beautiful was both your former festival, which you established on the sea, and if there is any other grace to the eyes, when I saw the sea covered with trees, and covered with a hand-made cloud, and the beauty of ships, and the speed, as if sent for a procession, and a moderate wind standing at the stern, as if escorting on purpose, and escorting to the city a city from the sea; but more beautiful and more magnificent is the one now seen.

choices.why: infinitive with negative contrasts former suffering with present refraining from harm, followed by power to do good and gentleness
θέλημα here is object of desire, you are what I desire, not the faculty of will

choices.term: ἐφ' ὃν παρατέτακται ὁ Κύριος τοῦ εὖ ποιῆσαι
choices.english: for whose benefit the Lord has been arrayed to do good
choices.why: ἐπί with accusative marks the beneficiary of protection, paired against evildoing to opponents
rejected: against whom the Lord is arrayed

choices.why: brief glossary requires equal honor for ὁμοτιμία
keeps literal γλύμμα as carved work without importing an unmarked scriptural identification

pass_b_english: On the contrary, danger only strengthened them, and they grew more zealous in reverence. Suffering for Christ does that: it deepens love, and for great souls it becomes a pledge of the contests still to come. Such are your stories and wonders in our own day, O Egypt.

You once praised to me the goats of Mendes, and Apis of Memphis, a fatted and fleshy calf, and the rites of Isis, and the dismemberments of Osiris, and your august Serapis, a piece of wood worshiped with the help of myth and age and the folly of its worshipers, as if it were some strange and heavenly matter, though matter still, even when falsehood comes to its aid. And there were things more shameful still, manifold images of beasts and creeping things. Christ rose above them all, and so did the preachers of Christ. Others shone in their own ways, each in his own time, and so did the Fathers just now remembered. From them you are known today, O wonderful one, more than all people together are known from all stories at once, old and new.

For this I embrace you and greet you, best of peoples, most loving of Christ, most fervent in reverence, and worthy of your leaders. I have nothing greater to say than this, and no better welcome to offer you. I receive you with a few movements of the tongue and many movements of the mind. You are my people. I call mine all who share the same mind and the same confession, who come from the same Fathers and worship the same Trinity. You are my people. You are mine, even if the envious deny it. And to sting those envious ones still more, see, I offer you the right hand of fellowship before so many witnesses, visible and invisible, and I drive away an old slander with a new kindness. You are my people. You are mine, even though I, the smallest, claim the greatest for my own. Such is the grace of the Spirit: it makes those who share one mind equal in honor. You are my people. You are mine, even from afar, for we are joined in a divine way, in another manner than bodily bulk allows. Bodies are joined by place, but souls are fitted together by the Spirit.

You are my people, who once made it your wisdom to suffer for Christ. Now, if you will listen to me, make it your wisdom not to act, but to count the very power to act as gain enough, and to offer gentleness to Christ as service, just as you once offered endurance. You are the people for whose benefit the Lord has arrayed himself to do good, as he is arrayed to do harm to his enemies. You are the people whom the Lord has chosen for himself out of all those he has called. You are the people painted on the hands of the Lord, to whom the Lord says, "For you are my delight," and, "Your gates are a carving," with all the other promises given afterward to those who are saved. You are my people, and do not wonder at my greed if I keep repeating your name. I delight in speaking it over and over, like those who can never have enough of some sight or sound.

O people of God, and mine as well, your earlier festival was beautiful, the one you held upon the sea, as much as any other delight for the eyes. I watched the sea turned into a forest of masts and covered with a handmade cloud, and saw the beauty of the ships and their speed, as if dispatched for a procession, with a gentle wind set behind the stern like an escort on purpose, convoying a seafaring city to our city. Yet the sight before us now is fairer and more magnificent.
notes: source spacing is damaged in ὑπερ ῆρε, ἄλ λως, δια νοίας, ψυ χαὶ, τρόπον ἄλλον separated, θα λάσσης; gloss follows the intended continuous forms
Αἱ πύλαι σου γλύμμα is obscure; gloss keeps what is written without identifying a verse
Σὺ γὰρ εἶ θέλημα ἐμὸν is glossed literally; no verse number is assigned

problems.quote: From them you learn today, O wonderful people, more than all people together learn from all stories at once, old and new.
problems.source_quote: ἀφ' ὧν σὺ γινώσκῃ μᾶλλον, ὦ θαυμασία, σήμερον, ἢ πάντων ὁμοῦ πάντες, καὶ παλαιῶν καὶ νέων διηγημάτων.
problems.why: Medio-passive γινώσκῃ means Egypt is known through the Fathers, not that Egypt learns.
problems.fix: From them you are known today, O wonderful one, more than all people together are known from every story, old and new.
problems.ruling: γινώσκῃ is passive (γινώσκῃ = 2nd sg. mid/pass 'you are known'); 'ἀφ' ὧν σὺ γινώσκῃ μᾶλλον' means Egypt is better known through the Fathers, not learning. Meaning reversed.

problems.quote: make it your wisdom not to do evil, but to count the very power to act as gain enough
problems.source_quote: νῦν δὲ τὸ μὴ ποιεῖν, ἐὰν ἐμοὶ πείθησθε, ἀλλ' αὔταρκες κέρδος τίθεσθαι τὴν τοῦ ποιεῖν ἐξουσίαν
problems.why: τὸ μὴ ποιεῖν is refraining from action, not refraining from evil. The power to act is the gain.
problems.fix: Now, if you heed me, make it your wisdom not to act, but to count the very power to act as gain enough.
problems.ruling: τὸ μὴ ποιεῖν has no 'evil' object; it means refraining from acting, matching 'τὴν τοῦ ποιεῖν ἐξουσίαν' (power to act). 'Evil' is added, changing the claim.

problems.quote: and any other delight for the eyes besides
problems.source_quote: καὶ εἴπερ ἄλλη τις ὀφθαλμῶν χάρις
problems.why: The source says the festival was beautiful, as much as any other delight for the eyes. The English turns this into a second, additional thing that was beautiful.
problems.fix: was beautiful, as much as any other delight for the eyes,
problems.ruling: καὶ εἴπερ ἄλλη τις ὀφθαλμῶν χάρις means “if any sight was delightful,” not a second beautiful thing beside the festival.

fixed: Passive γινώσκῃ and ô θαυμασία singular: Egypt is known through the Fathers, not learning.
Bare τὸ μὴ ποιεῖν is refraining from action, not from evil; power to act is the gain.
καὶ εἴπερ ἄλλη τις ὀφθαλμῶν χάρις makes the sea-festival as beautiful as any eye-delight, not an extra thing.

last_rejected.quote: And there were things more shameful still, manifold images of beasts and creeping things.
last_rejected.source_quote: καὶ τὰ ἔτι τούτων αἰσχρότερα, κνωδάλων τινῶν καὶ ἑρπετῶν πολυειδῆ πλάσματα
last_rejected.why: These images are still objects of “you praised.” English only says they existed.
last_rejected.fix: and, still more shameful, the manifold images of beasts and creeping things.
last_rejected.ruling: The English still reads as a continuation of the list of Egyptian cults. 'Christ rose above them all' follows, so the meaning survives. It is a minor loss of 'ἐπῄνεις' as governing verb.
